replacement: When the aristocratic morality goes astray and commits sacrilege against reality, it does so only in the one sphere it does not know well enough — a sphere, in fact, whose real knowledge it disdainfully keeps away from. In some cases it misjudges the sphere it despises, that of the common, vulgar man and the low people. But we should also weigh this: the mood of contempt, of disdain, of superciliousness, even if it falsely portrays the object of its contempt, will always be far from the degree of falsity that marks the attacks — in effigy, of course — which the vindictive hatred and revengefulness of the weak launch against their enemies. In fact, contempt contains too strong a mixture of nonchalance, of casualness, of boredom, of impatience, even of personal exultation, to be able to distort its victim into a real caricature or a real monstrosity. Notice again the almost benevolent shades of meaning which, for instance, the Greek nobility puts into all the words by which it distinguishes the common people from itself. See how a kind of pity, care, and consideration keeps lending them a honeyed flavor, until at last almost all the words applied to the vulgar man survive as expressions for "unhappy," "worthy of pity" (compare δειλο, δείλαιος, πονηρός, μοχθηρός]; the last two really name the vulgar man as labor-slave and beast of burden) — and see how, conversely, "bad," "low," "unhappy" have never stopped ringing in the Greek ear with a tone in which "unhappy" is the dominant note. This is a heritage of the old noble aristocratic morality, which stays true to itself even in contempt (let philologists remember the sense in which ὀιζυρός, ἄνολβος, τλήμων, δυστυχεῑν, ξυμφορά used to be employed). The "well-born" simply felt themselves to be the "happy"; they did not have to manufacture their happiness artificially by looking at their enemies, or, when need arose, talk and lie themselves into happiness (as all resentful men are accustomed to do). And being complete men, exuberant with strength and therefore necessarily energetic, they were too wise to separate happiness from action: for them activity necessarily counts as happiness (that is the etymology of εὖ πρἆττειν). All this stands in sharp contrast to the "happiness" of the weak and the oppressed, with their festering venom and malignity, among whom happiness appears essentially as a narcotic, a deadening, a quietude, a peace, a "Sabbath," a slackening of the mind and a relaxation of the limbs — in short, as a purely passive phenomenon. The aristocratic man lived in confidence and openness with himself (gennaios, "noble-born," stresses the shade of meaning "sincere," and perhaps also "naïf"). The resentful man, on the other hand, is neither sincere nor naïf, nor honest and candid with himself. His soul squints; his mind loves hidden crannies, tortuous paths and back-doors; everything secret appeals to him as his world, his safety, his balm. He is a past master in silence, in not forgetting, in waiting, in provisional self-depreciation and self-abasement. A race of such resentful men will necessarily end up more prudent than any aristocratic race. It will honor prudence on quite a different scale, as a paramount condition of existence. Among aristocratic men, by contrast, prudence tends to carry a delicate flavor of luxury and refinement; so it plays nothing like so essential a part among them as the complete certainty with which the governing unconscious instincts function, or even a certain lack of prudence, such as a vehement and valiant charge against danger or the enemy, or those ecstatic bursts of rage, love, reverence, and gratitude by which noble souls have at all times recognized each other. When the resentment of the aristocratic man shows itself, it fulfills and exhausts itself in an immediate reaction, and so it instills no venom. On the other hand, in countless cases it never shows itself at all, where in the feeble and weak it would be inevitable. An inability to take their enemies, their disasters, their misdeeds seriously for any length of time — that is the sign of the full, strong natures who possess a superfluity of molding, plastic force that heals completely and produces forgetfulness. A good example of this in the modern world is Mirabeau, who had no memory for the insults and meannesses practiced on him, and who could not forgive only because he forgot. Such a man shakes off with a shrug many a worm which would have buried itself in another; only in characters like these do we see the possibility (supposing, of course, that there is such a possibility in the world) of the real "love of one's enemies." How much respect for his enemies, forsooth, is found in an aristocratic man — and such reverence is already a bridge to love! He insists on having his enemy to himself as his distinction. He tolerates no enemy except one in whose character there is nothing to despise and much to honor! Now imagine, on the other hand, the "enemy" as the resentful man conceives him — and it is exactly here that we see his work, his creativeness. He has conceived "the evil enemy," the "evil one," and that is the root idea from which he then derives, as a contrasting and corresponding figure, a "good one": himself — his very self!

replacement: 11. This man's method is the exact opposite of the aristocrat's. The aristocrat forms the root idea "good" spontaneously, straight out of himself, and only then, from that material, creates for himself a concept of "bad"! This aristocratic "bad" and that "evil" from the cauldron of unsatisfied hatred are two very different things. The first is an imitation, an "extra," an additional nuance; the second is the original, the beginning, the essential act in the making of a slave-morality. Both "bad" and "evil" have the same opposite, "good," yet how great a difference they mark! For the idea "good" is not the same in each. Ask rather: "Who is really evil, according to the morality of resentment?" The answer, in all sternness, is this: just the good man of the other morality, just the aristocrat, the powerful one, the ruler, but seen through the venomous eye of resentfulness and so given a new color, a new meaning, a new look. We would be the last to deny this. A man who got to know those "good" ones only as enemies learned at the same time not to know them only as "evil enemies." Yet these same men are bound so rigorously inter pares by convention, respect, custom, and gratitude, and still more by mutual vigilance and jealousy inter pares. Among themselves they find so many new ways of showing consideration, self-control, delicacy, loyalty, pride, and friendship. But toward whatever lies outside their circle (where the foreign element, a foreign country, begins) they are not much better than beasts of prey let loose. There they are free of all social control. In the wilderness they can vent, with impunity, the tension built up by being fenced in and shut up within the peace of society. They revert to the innocence of the beast-of-prey conscience, like jubilant monsters who may be coming from a ghastly bout of murder, arson, rape, and torture, with bravado and moral equanimity, as if it were merely some wild student's prank, fully convinced that the poets now have plenty to sing and celebrate. At the core of all these aristocratic races we cannot fail to recognize the beast of prey, the magnificent blond brute, greedily prowling for spoil and victory. This hidden core needed an outlet from time to time; the beast had to get loose again and return to the wilderness. The Roman, Arabic, German, and Japanese nobility, the Homeric heroes, the Scandinavian Vikings, all share this need. The aristocratic races left the idea "Barbarian" behind on every path they marched. Nay, a consciousness of this very barbarianism, and even a pride in it, shows itself in their highest civilization (for example, when Pericles tells his Athenians in the celebrated funeral oration, "Our audacity has forced a way over every land and sea, rearing everywhere imperishable memorials of itself for good and for evil"). The audacity of aristocratic races may be mad, absurd, and spasmodic in its expression; their enterprises may be incalculable and fantastic — Pericles sets in special relief and glory the ᾽ραθυμία of the Athenians, their nonchalance and contempt for safety, body, life, and comfort, their awful joy and intense delight in all destruction, in all the ecstasies of victory and cruelty — all these features crystallized, for those who suffered from them, into the picture of the "barbarian," of the "evil enemy," perhaps of the "Goth" and the "Vandal." Even now, the German meets a profound, icy mistrust as soon as he comes to power. That mistrust is still an aftermath of the inextinguishable horror with which Europe, for whole centuries, regarded the wrath of the blond Teuton beast (although there is scarcely a psychological, let alone a physical, relationship between the old Germans and ourselves). I once pointed out Hesiod's embarrassment when he conceived the series of social ages and tried to express them in gold, silver, and bronze. The Homeric world confronted him with a contradiction: an age magnificent indeed, but at the same time so awful and so violent. He could resolve it only by making two ages out of one and setting them one behind the other. First came the age of the heroes and demigods, as that world lived on in the memories of the aristocratic families, who found their own ancestors in it. Then came the bronze age, as that same age looked to the descendants of the oppressed, spoiled, ill-treated, exiled, and enslaved: an age of bronze, as I have said, hard, cold, terrible, without feelings and without conscience, crushing everything and spattering everything with blood. Suppose the now-accepted theory is true, that the whole essence of civilization is to train the beast of prey out of man and make of him a tame and civilized animal, a domesticated animal. Then we must undoubtedly regard as the real tools of civilization all those instincts of reaction and resentment, with whose help the aristocratic races, together with their ideals, were finally degraded and overpowered. That is not yet to say that the bearers of those tools also represented civilization. The opposite is not merely probable — nay, it is palpable today. These bearers of vindictive instincts that have to be bottled up, these descendants of all European and non-European slavery, especially of the pre-Aryan population — these people, I say, represent the decline of humanity! These "tools of civilization" are a disgrace to humanity, and in reality they count more as an argument against civilization, more as a reason to be suspicious of it. One may be quite justified in always fearing the blond beast at the core of every aristocratic race, and in staying on one's guard. But who would not a hundred times rather fear, while admiring, than be free of fear and be forever obsessed with the loathsome sight of the distorted, the dwarfed, the stunted, the envenomed? And is that not our fate? What makes us feel repulsion toward "man" today? — for we suffer from "man," there is no doubt about it. It is not fear. It is rather that we have nothing left to fear from men; that the worm "man" is in the foreground and swarms; that the "tame man," the wretched, mediocre, unedifying creature, has learned to consider himself a goal and a pinnacle, an inner meaning, a historic principle, a "higher man." Yes, and he has a certain right to do so, in so far as he feels that, set against that excess of deformity, disease, exhaustion, and effeteness whose odor is beginning to pollute present-day Europe, he at any rate has achieved a relative success; he at any rate still says "yes" to life.

replacement: 15. In the faith in what? In the love for what? In the hope of what? These weaklings! — they also, forsooth, wish to be the strong some time; there is no doubt about it, some time their kingdom also must come — "the kingdom of God" is their name for it, as has been mentioned: they are so meek in everything! Yet to experience that kingdom one has to live long, to live beyond death — yes, eternal life is necessary, so that one can make up forever for that earthly life "in faith," "in love," "in hope." Make up for what? Make up by what? Dante, it seems to me, made a crass mistake when, with awe-inspiring ingenuity, he placed the inscription "Me too made eternal love" over the gate of his hell. At any rate, the inscription "Me too made eternal hate" would have a much better right to stand over the gate of the Christian Paradise and its "eternal blessedness" — granted, of course, that a truth may rightly stand over the gate to a lie! For what is the blessedness of that Paradise? Possibly we could quickly guess it; but it is better to have it explicitly attested by an authority not to be disparaged in such matters, Thomas of Aquinas, the great teacher and saint. "Beati in regno celesti" he says, as gently as a lamb, "videbunt pœnas damnatorum, ut beatitudo illis magis complaceat." Or if we wish to hear a stronger tone, here is a word from the mouth of a triumphant father of the Church, who warned his disciples against the cruel ecstasies of the public spectacles — But why? Faith offers us much more, he says, de Spectac., c. 29 ss., something much stronger. Thanks to the redemption, joys of quite another kind are at our disposal; instead of athletes we have our martyrs; if we wish for blood, well, we have the blood of Christ — but what then awaits us on the day of his return, of his triumph. And then he goes on, this enraptured visionary: "at enim supersunt alia spectacula, ille ultimas et perpetuus judicii dies, ille nationibus insperatus, ille derisus, cum tanta sæculi vetustas et tot ejus nativitates uno igne haurientur. Quæ tunc spectaculi latitudo! Quid admirer! quid rideam! Ubigaudeam! Ubi exultem, spectans tot et tantos reges, qui in cœlum recepti nuntiabantur, cum ipso Jove et ipsis suis testibus in imis tenebris congemescentes! Item præsides" (the provincial governors) "persecutores dominici nominis sævioribus quam ipsi flammis sævierunt insultantibus contra Christianos liquescentes! Quos præterea sapientes illos philosophos coram discipulis suis una conflagrantibus erubescentes, quibus nihil ad deum pertinere suadebant, quibus animas aut nullas aut non in pristina corpora redituras affirmabant! Etiam poetas non ad Rhadamanti nec ad Minois, sed ad inopinati Christi tribunal palpitantes! Tunc magis tragœdi audiendi, magis scilicet vocales" (with louder tones and more violent shrieks) "in sua propria calamitate; tunc histriones cognoscendi, solutiores multo per ignem; tunc spectandus auriga in flammea rota totus rubens, tunc xystici contemplandi non in gymnasiis, sed in igne jaculati, nisi quod ne tunc quidem illos velim vivos, ut qui malim ad eos potius conspectum insatiabilem conferre, qui in dominum scevierunt. Hic est ille, dicam fabri aut quæstuariæ filius" (as the whole of the following shows, and in particular this well-known description of the mother of Jesus from the Talmud, Tertullian is from here on referring to the Jews), "sabbati destructor, Samarites et dæmonium habens. Hic est quem a Juda redemistis, hic est ille arundine et colaphis diverberatus, sputamentis de decoratus, felle et acete potatus. Hic est, quem clam discentes subripuerunt, ut resurrexisse dicatur vel hortulanus detraxit, ne lactucæ suæ frequentia commeantium laderentur. Ut talia species, ut talibus exultes, quis tibi prætor aut consul aut sacerdos de sua liberalitate prastabit? Et tamen hæc jam habemus quodammodo per fidem spiritu imaginante repræsentata. Ceterum qualia illa sunt, quæ nec oculus vidit nec auris audivit nec in cor hominis ascenderunt?" (I Cor. ii. 9.) "Credo circo et utraque cavea" (the first and fourth row, or, according to others, the comic and the tragic stage) "et omni studio gratiora." Per fidem: so it stands written.

note: Parenthetical aside listing the four figures was turned into a colon list with an added "You bow to"; asides must stay in parentheses.
replacement: Which of them has been victorious for the time being, Rome or Judæa? There is not a shadow of doubt. Just consider whom you bow down to even in Rome itself today, as though to the quintessence of all the highest values — and not only in Rome, but over almost half the world, wherever man has been tamed or is about to be tamed. You bow to three Jews, as we know, and one Jewess (Jesus of Nazareth, Peter the fisher, Paul the tent-maker, and the mother of the aforesaid Jesus, named Mary). This is very remarkable: Rome is undoubtedly defeated. At any rate, in the Renaissance there was a brilliantly sinister revival of the classical ideal, of the aristocratic valuation of all things. Rome herself, like a man waking from a trance, stirred under the weight of the new Judaized Rome built over her, which looked like an œcumenical synagogue and was called the "Church." But Judæa immediately triumphed again, thanks to that fundamentally popular (German and English) movement of revenge called the Reformation, and thanks also to its inevitable corollary, the restoration of the Church — which also restored the ancient graveyard peace of classical Rome. In the French Revolution Judæa again proved victorious over the classical ideal, in a sense even more crucial and more profound. The last political aristocracy in Europe, that of seventeenth- and eighteenth-century France, broke into pieces under the instincts of a resentful populace. The world had never heard a greater jubilation, a more uproarious enthusiasm. Yet in the midst of it the most monstrous and unexpected thing happened: the ancient ideal itself rose before the eyes and conscience of humanity with all its life and with unheard-of splendor. Against resentment's lying war-cry of the prerogative of the most, against the will to lowliness, abasement, and equalization, the will to a retrogression and twilight of humanity, there rang out once more, stronger, simpler, and more penetrating than ever, the terrible and enchanting counter-warcry of the prerogative of the few! Then, like a final signpost to other ways, Napoleon appeared, the most unique and violent anachronism that ever existed, and in him the incarnate problem of the aristocratic ideal in itself. Consider well what a problem it is: Napoleon, that synthesis of Monster and Superman.

Note. — This treatise gives me the opportunity to express, openly and formally, a wish I have so far voiced only in occasional conversations with scholars. I wish that some Faculty of philosophy would earn the glory of promoting further study of the history of morals through a series of prize essays; perhaps this book may give a forceful impetus in that direction. For such a possibility, the following question deserves consideration. It deserves the attention of philologists and historians quite as much as that of actual professional philosophers.
